title: For Industrial Companies, Winning with AI Takes More Than Tech
gist: BCG argues the industrial productivity playbook is exhausted (US industrial labor productivity -1.2%/yr since 2014) and that AI only pays off when firms reshape organizations rather than deploy copilots, since ~70% of AI value comes from people/process/org changes that ~70% of US industrial adopters skip. Building a company-specific 'enterprise cortex' and going fully AI-first could lift EBIT margins 2.5-5.6pp in chemicals, automotive and A&D, with org changes taking 18-24 months.

insights.claim: US industrial labor productivity has fallen at an annualized 1.2% since 2014, while productivity across all other US sectors rose by an average of 1.2%; manufacturing productivity has also declined in Europe's largest industrial economies.
insights.speaker: Minjee Kim
insights.so_what: The lean/six-sigma/robotics productivity engine is exhausted, so industrial margin expansion now needs a new lever rather than more of the old playbook.
insights.quote: Among US industrial companies, labor productivity has fallen by an annualized 1.2% since 2014 even as productivity across all other sectors has increased by an average of 1.2%.
insights.locator: For decades, industrial players have turned

insights.claim: BCG argues the decades-old industrial productivity playbook of robotics, lean manufacturing and six sigma has 'run its course', with labor productivity in industrials declining across the largest advanced economies since peaking around the mid-2010s.
insights.speaker: Minjee Kim
insights.so_what: Investors should discount operational-excellence narratives built on incremental lean programs as a source of future margin gains.
insights.quote: This playbook has run its course, however.
insights.locator: For decades, industrial players have turned

insights.claim: Lean and six sigma trained industrial companies to improve stable, standardized processes in small controlled steps, which is mismatched to AI-first operations that require redesigning processes end to end and then redesigning again as technology evolves; BCG says organizational adaptation speed, not technology, sets the pace of AI value creation in industrials.
insights.speaker: Minjee Kim
insights.so_what: Historic excellence in lean culture may be a hidden liability for AI adoption; judge industrials on org-change velocity rather than tech spend.
insights.quote: In our experience, the speed at which an organization can adapt plays a bigger role in setting the pace of AI value creation in industrials than the technology does.
insights.locator: The Organization Issue

insights.claim: Deploying copilots and assistants into unchanged workflows saves individual industrial workers an estimated 10%-15% of task time, but much of that gain never reaches the P&L because the saved time is absorbed elsewhere.
insights.speaker: Minjee Kim
insights.so_what: Copilot-seat rollouts are weak evidence of earnings impact; look for headcount, throughput or cost-line changes instead.
insights.quote: Much of that gain rarely shows up in the P&L, because the time saved gets absorbed elsewhere.
insights.locator: Three AI Pathways in Industrials

insights.claim: Reshaping core functions end to end around agentic AI, with agents executing most work and humans supervising, can deliver a 30%-50% improvement in function efficiency and effectiveness, versus 10%-15% from simple tool deployment.
insights.speaker: Minjee Kim
insights.so_what: The gap between deploy and reshape is roughly 3x in functional uplift, which is where AI leaders' earnings divergence will come from.
insights.quote: Reshaping core functions in this way can deliver a 30% to 50% improvement in their efficiency and effectiveness.
insights.locator: Three AI Pathways in Industrials

insights.claim: BCG frames industrial AI adoption as three pathways - Deploy (tools assisting humans in unchanged processes), Reshape (end-to-end workflow and org redesign) and Invent (new data-based business models and value pools) - and says simple deployment is becoming table stakes.
insights.speaker: Minjee Kim
insights.so_what: Use the deploy/reshape/invent ladder to classify management AI claims; only reshape and invent are differentiating.
insights.quote: Introducing the technology into existing workflows has its place, but the approach is becoming table stakes in AI adoption.
insights.locator: Three AI Pathways in Industrials: Deploy, Reshape, and Invent

insights.claim: In BCG's AI transformation work, value splits roughly 10-20-70: about 10% from algorithms, 20% from technology and data, and 70% from people, organization and processes ('the 70').
insights.speaker: Minjee Kim
insights.so_what: Vendors of models and infrastructure capture a minority of transformation value; the bulk accrues to firms able to execute org change.
insights.quote: In the AI transformations we have worked on, value splits roughly 10-20-70.
insights.locator: Nevertheless, most industrial companies still deploy

insights.claim: According to US Census Bureau information, almost 70% of US industrial companies that adopt AI make no organizational, data or process changes, and only 12% build new workflows versus nearly one-third of information-sector companies.
insights.speaker: Minjee Kim
insights.so_what: Most industrial AI adopters are leaving the largest value bucket untouched, implying a long runway of dispersion between leaders and laggards.
insights.quote: almost 70% of US industrial companies that adopt AI make no organizational, data, or process changes; and only 12% build new workflows, versus nearly one-third of information companies.
insights.locator: Nevertheless, most industrial companies still deploy

insights.claim: Industrial AI leaders grew revenues more than twice as fast as sector AI laggards from 2022 to 2025, delivered roughly double the three-year TSR, and captured over twice the share of AI-enabled cost savings.
insights.speaker: Minjee Kim
insights.so_what: AI maturity is already showing up as revenue and TSR dispersion within industrials, supporting a long-leaders/short-laggards framing.
insights.quote: they grew revenues more than twice as fast as the sector’s AI laggards from 2022 to 2025 and delivered roughly double the three-year TSR.
insights.locator: AI leaders in industrials are already doing this

insights.claim: Per the BCG Applied AI Index 2026, the most AI-mature companies across sectors ('future-built for AI') achieved a 12% revenue CAGR, a 14% EBITDA CAGR, and a 54% three-year TSR from 2022 to 2025.
insights.speaker: Minjee Kim
insights.so_what: Benchmarks for what AI-mature performance looks like; note it is a consultancy survey with likely selection effects.
insights.locator: For decades, industrial players have turned

insights.claim: A chemical company added sensors to office hand sanitizer bottles and used AI to predict replacement needs, converting a commodity sanitizer sale into a higher-margin sanitizer-as-a-service business.
insights.speaker: Minjee Kim
insights.so_what: Example of the 'Invent' pathway: sensor+AI turns product sales into recurring service revenue with better margins.
insights.locator: Moving beyond simple deployment also enables

themes.theme: Why industrials lag: data and trust

insights.claim: Only 12% of industrial companies have the data capabilities needed to be future-built for AI versus an 18% average across other sectors, with the biggest gap in data strategy; industrials are also less likely to expect AI agents to have decision-making autonomy by 2030.
insights.speaker: Minjee Kim
insights.so_what: Industrials structurally trail other sectors on AI readiness, so sector-wide AI margin uplift will arrive later and more unevenly.
insights.quote: only 12% of industrial companies have the necessary data capabilities to be future-built for AI, compared with an average of 18% across all other sectors
insights.locator: The Trust Issue

insights.claim: Industrial data is hard to use for AI because it is siloed across functions and sites, much practical insight lives undocumented in senior managers' heads, and multitiered supply chains, extensive bills of materials and multi-market regulation add complexity vendors often won't share data on.
insights.speaker: Minjee Kim
insights.so_what: Data-layer and sensorization spend is a prerequisite capex for industrial AI, favoring firms already invested in connected assets.
insights.quote: Practical insights reside in senior managers’ heads rather than being documented.
insights.locator: The Data Issue

insights.claim: BCG warns that widespread use of off-the-shelf external AI models risks 'cognitive lock-in', where generic models come to dictate how companies make decisions.
insights.speaker: Minjee Kim
insights.so_what: Reliance on commodity models erodes differentiation; proprietary decision logic becomes the defensible asset.
insights.locator: The Enterprise Cortex’s Central Role

insights.claim: BCG's 'enterprise cortex' is a company-specific layer in the AI stack that links business functions and codifies the firm's business rules, decision logic and operational context, giving agents shared definitions and guardrails; BCG argues industrials need it even more than other sectors due to siloed data and harsher consequences of agent errors.
insights.speaker: Minjee Kim
insights.so_what: Look for industrials investing in codified decision-logic layers, not just model access, as the marker of durable AI advantage.
insights.quote: we believe that industrial companies need an enterprise cortex even more than most other sectors do.
insights.locator: The Enterprise Cortex’s Central Role

insights.claim: Because models and computing power are equally available to competitors, BCG argues neither the number of agents nor data volume differentiates a company; differentiation comes from how much proprietary know-how is codified and connected to agents.
insights.speaker: Minjee Kim
insights.so_what: AI moats in industrials will be firm-specific process knowledge, implying commoditization of model/compute layers for end users.
insights.quote: Since models and computing power are equally available to competitors, neither the number of agents nor the volume of data will set a company apart from others.
insights.locator: Five Must-Do Actions for Senior Leaders

insights.claim: The 'AI-first matrix' sets agent autonomy by asking whether AI can do a task (performance vs people) and whether it should (stakes of error); where AI is capable but stakes are high, such as a certificate of release, the mode is 'AI flies, humans land' - agents prepare, a qualified person decides.
insights.speaker: Minjee Kim
insights.so_what: A practical lens for judging which industrial workflows can be automated soon versus remaining human-gated.
insights.locator: The Enterprise Cortex’s Central Role

insights.claim: BCG calls the chemical industry's situation a structural crisis rather than a cyclical dip: TSRs are bottom-quartile among asset-heavy industries, EBIT margins and ROCE have declined for over a decade, and overcapacity in ethylene, propylene and aromatics is expected to persist through 2030.
insights.speaker: Minjee Kim
insights.so_what: Don't underwrite a cyclical recovery in commodity petrochemicals before 2030; favor players with self-help levers like AI over capacity cuts.
insights.quote: The chemical industry faces a structural crisis, not a cyclical dip.
insights.locator: Deep Dive: The AI-First Chemicals Company

insights.claim: Raw materials and energy typically make up 65%-75% of chemical companies' total costs, so AI value in chemicals concentrates in R&D, manufacturing operations/supply chain, and marketing and sales rather than headcount.
insights.speaker: Minjee Kim
insights.so_what: AI margin levers in chemicals are about yield, energy and pricing optimization against a feedstock-dominated cost base.
insights.quote: The chemical industry’s cost base is dominated by raw materials and energy, which typically account for 65% to 75% of total costs.
insights.locator: Deep Dive: The AI-First Chemicals Company

insights.claim: In continuous chemical processes such as crackers and distillation columns, AI can keep plants at their economic optimum by continuously resetting setpoints based on live margin, energy price and process constraints, with agents writing approved setpoint changes directly into control systems within a defined envelope.
insights.speaker: Minjee Kim
insights.so_what: Self-optimizing plants make margin capture more responsive to energy-price swings, a competitive edge in volatile feedstock markets.
insights.locator: Manufacturing Operations, Including Supply Chain

insights.claim: A polymer producer using AI planning agents to evaluate 50,000 planning scenarios over a 60-day horizon improved gross margin by $8-$10 per ton and customer service levels by 4%.
insights.speaker: Minjee Kim
insights.so_what: Concrete per-ton margin evidence for AI planning in commodity chemicals.
insights.quote: A polymer producer that used AI planning agents to evaluate 50,000 planning scenarios over a 60-day horizon improved gross margin by $8 to $10 per ton and customer service levels by 4%.
insights.locator: Manufacturing Operations, Including Supply Chain

insights.claim: A global specialty chemicals distributor using AI-supported sales generated 30-40 new leads per rep per month and raised EBITDA contribution from pilot segments by 3%-5%.
insights.speaker: Minjee Kim
insights.so_what: AI sales tooling has measurable EBITDA impact in specialty distribution, where cross-sell matters.
insights.locator: Manufacturing Operations, Including Supply Chain

insights.claim: Specialty chemical players can use AI to monitor product performance in customers' processes and shift from selling product to selling outcomes - e.g., a water-treatment specialist charging for avoided downtime rather than tons of chemicals - adding recurring revenue.
insights.speaker: Minjee Kim
insights.so_what: Outcome-based models could re-rate specialty chemicals toward service-like recurring revenue multiples.
insights.quote: charge for avoided downtime rather than for tons of chemicals.
insights.locator: Manufacturing Operations, Including Supply Chain

insights.claim: BCG models that large, global, strong-performing chemical companies reshaping to become AI-first may improve EBIT margin by 2.5-4.5 percentage points, with technology/IT the only cost line deliberately increased.
insights.speaker: Minjee Kim
insights.so_what: A sizeable self-help margin lever for a sector facing overcapacity, but rising IT/compute cost is the trade-off.
insights.locator: Our modeling suggests that large, global

insights.claim: The commercial aerospace backlog stands at roughly 17,000 aircraft, about 12 years of production at current rates; engine shop visit demand is projected to exceed capacity by 15%-20% by 2030, certified technician shortage to reach 20% by 2028, and roughly three in four programs are missing ramp-up timelines.
insights.speaker: Minjee Kim
insights.so_what: A&D is supply-constrained, so AI's main value is throughput, not cost; capacity bottlenecks support aftermarket pricing power.
insights.quote: The commercial backlog stands at roughly 17,000 aircraft—about 12 years of production at current rates.
insights.locator: Deep Dive: The AI-First Aerospace and Defense Company

insights.claim: Across 12 listed A&D companies, airframer original equipment generates about 20% of revenue and none of the profit, while engines and aftermarket services generate 29% of revenue and more than half of the profit.
insights.speaker: Minjee Kim
insights.so_what: Profit pools sit in engines and aftermarket; AI-driven gains widen the gap further in favor of installed-base businesses.
insights.quote: airframer original equipment generates about 20% of revenue and none of the profit, while engines and aftermarket services generate 29% of revenue and more than half of the profit.
insights.locator: Deep Dive: The AI-First Aerospace and Defense Company

insights.claim: Commercial A&D R&D is self-funded so AI savings flow to margin, whereas defense development is largely customer-funded and cost-type savings pass to the government; BCG estimates defense-heavy portfolios realize roughly half the AI margin uplift.
insights.speaker: Minjee Kim
insights.so_what: Expect AI margin upside to accrue to commercial-heavy over defense-heavy A&D portfolios.
insights.quote: Defense-heavy portfolios realize roughly half of this enhancement after cost-type passthrough.
insights.locator: Our modeling suggests an EBIT margin improvement

insights.claim: BCG models AI-first EBIT margin improvement of about 3.3 percentage points for established A&D OEMs and 5.6 points for aftermarket businesses, with technology spend roughly doubling to fund the data layer and agent tooling.
insights.speaker: Minjee Kim
insights.so_what: Aftermarket/MRO-heavy names have the largest modeled AI margin upside in industrials.
insights.quote: Our modeling suggests an EBIT margin improvement of about 3.3 percentage points for established OEMs and 5.6 percentage points for aftermarket businesses
insights.locator: Our modeling suggests an EBIT margin improvement

insights.claim: Engine OEMs are using machine-learning surrogates to test hundreds of thousands of design combinations in milliseconds; one company reports halving design lead times in some cases, one rolled out an AI blade inspection tool that halved turbine-blade inspection times, and another bought an AI software firm that reads borescope video.
insights.speaker: Minjee Kim
insights.so_what: AI is already compressing engine design and MRO inspection cycles, supporting aftermarket capacity.
insights.locator: Engineering and Certification

insights.claim: During a widebody ramp-up, one airframer linked engineering, production and supplier data via AI, resolving quality issues faster and cutting delivery lead times by a third.
insights.speaker: Minjee Kim
insights.so_what: Evidence that data-linking can relieve ramp-up bottlenecks central to A&D delivery shortfalls.
insights.locator: Engineering and Certification

insights.claim: BCG argues AI-first value in A&D compounds along the chain - better engineering data lifts first-pass yield, which makes production plans credible so suppliers commit, while fleet growth feeds aftermarket forecasts back into planning - and a weak link limits everything downstream, which is why isolated pilots rarely scale.
insights.speaker: Minjee Kim
insights.so_what: Favor integrated, end-to-end AI programs over point pilots when assessing A&D execution.
insights.quote: Conversely, a weak link limits everything downstream, which is one reason why isolated pilots rarely scale.
insights.locator: The value of being an AI-first player compounds

themes.theme: Automotive OEMs: materials, S&OP, China speed

insights.claim: BCG says automotive AI value sits in core processes rather than support functions, with a full 3-5 percentage point EBIT margin uplift driven mainly by S&OP, sales, R&D and sourcing - largely by lowering material costs, which equal roughly 57% of revenues, not by cutting headcount.
insights.speaker: Minjee Kim
insights.so_what: Auto AI value is a procurement/materials story; headcount-cut narratives miss the main lever.
insights.quote: The value that AI creates is not primarily about replacing headcount; to a large degree, it involves lowering material costs, which are equivalent to roughly 57% of revenues.
insights.locator: Deep Dive: The AI-First Automotive OEM Company

insights.claim: Agentic S&OP at automotive OEMs, forecasting demand continuously instead of every four weeks and reconciling supply and demand in parallel, yields a 15%-20% drop in inventory and a 40% reduction in planning effort.
insights.speaker: Minjee Kim
insights.so_what: Inventory release is a working-capital tailwind for OEMs that adopt agentic planning.
insights.quote: The result is a 15% to 20% drop in inventory and a 40% reduction in planning effort.
insights.locator: S&OP

insights.claim: Chinese OEMs can launch a new vehicle in about 20-24 months while some Western incumbents still take three to four years; BCG sees AI-driven R&D (coding agents, agentic CAD) as a key lever for Western OEMs to match China's speed-to-market, along with a 1%-2% cut in overall materials costs.
insights.speaker: Minjee Kim
insights.so_what: Western auto incumbents face a structural speed gap; AI R&D adoption is a key watch item for their competitiveness.
insights.quote: Chinese OEMs can launch a new vehicle in approximately 20 to 24 months, whereas some Western incumbents still take three to four years.
insights.locator: R&D

insights.claim: Falling token costs are rapidly expanding what agentic AI can do in automotive, moving agentic transformation from an IT initiative to the C-suite agenda, with agents becoming an operating layer coordinating across systems via standardized protocols.
insights.speaker: Minjee Kim
insights.so_what: Cheaper inference broadens agent use cases, supporting demand for agent tooling and compute in industrial end markets.
insights.quote: Thanks to falling token costs, the range of what agentic AI can do is expanding fast.
insights.locator: Deep Dive: The AI-First Automotive OEM Company

insights.claim: OEMs that use AI to guide buyers from first search to signed contract should sell more cars mainly by taking share from slower rivals, lifting profits through volume without changing margin structure.
insights.speaker: Minjee Kim
insights.so_what: AI-driven sales is a share-shift game in autos; laggards lose volume.
insights.locator: Marketing and Sales. AI-driven pricing engines

insights.claim: Across chemicals, automotive and aerospace and defense, BCG models that companies fully reshaping as AI-first could raise EBIT margin by roughly 2.5 to 5.6 percentage points at maturity.
insights.speaker: Minjee Kim
insights.so_what: Size of the potential industrial AI margin prize; a key gauge of upside for successful adopters.
insights.locator: Five Must-Do Actions for Senior Leaders

insights.claim: Key organizational changes for AI-first transformation typically take 18-24 months to land, running as a multiyear program in iterative waves that becomes self-funding from year two.
insights.speaker: Minjee Kim
insights.so_what: Earnings benefits from industrial AI reshaping lag by ~2 years; early movers gain a time-based advantage.
insights.quote: Key organizational changes typically take 18 to 24 months to land, and they need to start now.
insights.locator: Capturing value from AI requires investment

insights.claim: Because agent expertise is replicable wherever needed, BCG expects industrials to reorganize around outcomes with end-to-end processes owned by one accountable person and run by humans plus agents, resulting in fewer management layers, consolidated functions and a workforce mix tilted to tech talent.
insights.speaker: Minjee Kim
insights.so_what: Expect middle-management de-layering and rising tech-talent demand at AI-first industrials.
insights.locator: Five Must-Do Actions for Senior Leaders

insights.claim: BCG says AI reshaping stalls without top-down leadership: the CEO must own the program rather than delegating to IT, and boards need AI-literate members able to challenge AI strategy.
insights.speaker: Minjee Kim
insights.so_what: Governance signals (CEO ownership, board AI literacy) are leading indicators of which industrials will capture AI value.
insights.locator: Five Must-Do Actions for Senior Leaders
